q-65204.name: Question 1
q-65204.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy).$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
q-65204.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡xy \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(0,\frac{\pi }{2})={f}_{y}(0,\frac{\pi }{2})i-{f}_{x}(0,\frac{\pi }{2})j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))\,j \\ t(0,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-0\operatorname{cos}⁡(0\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}))j \\  & =-i+\frac{\pi }{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-i+\frac{\pi }{2}\,j.$

Question 1
?

Consider the plane curve cos⁡xcos⁡y=sin⁡(xy). Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point (0,π2).

a
−i−j
b
i+π2j
c
−π2i−j
d
−i+π2j
e
−π2i+j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: cos⁡xcos⁡y=sin⁡xycos⁡xcos⁡y−sin⁡(xy)=0

If we set f(x,y)=cos⁡xcos⁡y−sin⁡xy, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point (0,π2) can be computed as follows: t(0,π2)=fy(0,π2)i−fx(0,π2)j

So, we calculate t(x,y) and evaluate it at (0,π2):

t(x,y)=∂∂y(cos⁡xcos⁡y−sin⁡(xy))i−∂∂x(cos⁡xcos⁡y−sin⁡(xy))j=(−cos⁡xsin⁡y−xcos⁡(xy))i−(−sin⁡xcos⁡y−ycos⁡(xy))jt(0,π2)=(−cos⁡(0)sin⁡(π2)−0cos⁡(0⋅π2))i−(−sin⁡(0)cos⁡(π2)−π2cos⁡(0⋅π2))j=−i+π2j

Therefore, our tangent vector is −i+π2j.

q-65208.name: Question 2
q-65208.problem: At which points on the curve $9{x}^{2}y=3{y}^{3}-6x$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$
q-65208.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}y & =3{y}^{3}-6x \\ 9{x}^{2}y-3{y}^{3}+6x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=9{x}^{2}y-3{y}^{3}+6x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(9{x}^{2}y-3{y}^{3}+6x)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(9{x}^{2}y-3{y}^{3}+6x)j \\  & =(9{x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})i-(18xy+6)j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot i=0.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((9{x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})\,i-(18xy+6)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 9{x}^{2}-9{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2} \\ y & =\pm x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-x$ into the equation of our curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}y & =3{y}^{3}{x}^{2}-6x \\ 9{x}^{2}(-x) & =3(-x)^{3}-6x \\ -9{x}^{3} & =-3{x}^{3}-6x \\ -6{x}^{3}+6x & =0 \\ 6x(1-{x}^{2}) & =0 \\ x & =0\,\text{or}\,x=\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the equation of our curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}y & =3{y}^{3}{x}^{2}-6x \\ 9{x}^{2}(x) & =3(x)^{3}-6x \\ 9{x}^{3} & =3{x}^{3}-6x \\ 6{x}^{3}+6x & =0 \\ 6x(1+{x}^{2}) & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=0$, we get that $y=0$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=1$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,1).$

- If $x=1$, we get $y=-1$ and the corresponding point is $(1,-1).$

q-65208.html:
Question 2
?

At which points on the curve 9x2y=3y3−6x is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector i?

a
(0,0) and (1,1) only
b
(0,0), (−1,−1), and (1,1)
c
(0,0) and (1,−1) only
d
(1,−1) only
e
(0,0), (−1,1), and (1,−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: 9x2y=3y3−6x9x2y−3y3+6x=0

If we set f(x,y)=9x2y−3y3+6x, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows: t(x,y)=fy(x,y)i−fx(x,y)j

So, we calculate t(x,y):

t(x,y)=fy(x,y)i−fx(x,y)j=∂∂y(9x2y−3y3+6x)i−∂∂x(9x2y−3y3+6x)j=(9x2−9y2)i−(18xy+6)j

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to i, we must have t⋅i=0.

t(x,y)⋅i=0((9x2−9y2)i−(18xy+6)j)⋅i=09x2−9y2=0y2=x2y=±x

Substituting y=−x into the equation of our curve gives:

9x2y=3y3x2−6x9x2(−x)=3(−x)3−6x−9x3=−3x3−6x−6x3+6x=06x(1−x2)=0x=0orx=±1

Substituting y=x into the equation of our curve gives:

9x2y=3y3x2−6x9x2(x)=3(x)3−6x9x3=3x3−6x6x3+6x=06x(1+x2)=0x=0

Finally:

  • If x=0, we get that y=0 and the corresponding point is (0,0).

  • If x=−1, we get y=1 and the corresponding point is (−1,1).

  • If x=1, we get y=−1 and the corresponding point is (1,−1).

q-65209.name: Question 3
q-65209.problem: At which points on the curve $3y{x}^{2}=48+3x{y}^{2}$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i-j?$
q-65209.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y{x}^{2} & =48+3x{y}^{2} \\ 3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2} & =48\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=48.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2})i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(3y{x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2})j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}-6xy)i-(6xy-3{y}^{2})j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i$, we must have $t\cdot (i-j)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot (i-j) & =0 \\ ((3{x}^{2}-6xy)i-(6xy-3{y}^{2})j)\cdot (i-j) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-6xy+6xy-3{y}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-y)(x+y) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=y$ or $x=-y.$ Substituting $x=y$ into the equation of our curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y{x}^{2} & =48+3x{y}^{2} \\ 3y{y}^{2} & =48+3y{y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{3} & =48+3{y}^{3} \\ 0 & =48\end{aligned}
$$

Since we get a false statement, we conclude that does not exist points of the form $(x,x)$ on the curve. Substituting $x=-y$ into the equation of our curve gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y{x}^{2} & =48+3x{y}^{2} \\ 3y(-y)^{2} & =48+3(-y){y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{3} & =48-3{y}^{3} \\ 6{y}^{3} & =48 \\ {y}^{3} & =8 \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{8} \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $y=2$, we get $x=-2$ and the corresponding point is $(-2,2).$

q-65209.html:
Question 3
?

At which points on the curve 3yx2=48+3xy2 is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector i−j?

a
(−2,2) only
b
(2,2) only
c
(−43,43) and (43,−43)
d
(−43,43) and (2,2)
e
(−43,43) and (−2,−2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: 3yx2=48+3xy23yx2−3xy2=48

If we set f(x,y)=3yx2−3xy2, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=48.

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows: t(x,y)=fy(x,y)i−fx(x,y)j

So, we calculate t(x,y):

t(x,y)=fy(x,y)i−fx(x,y)j=∂∂y(3yx2−3xy2)i−∂∂x(3yx2−3xy2)j=(3x2−6xy)i−(6xy−3y2)j

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to i, we must have t⋅(i−j)=0.

t(x,y)⋅(i−j)=0((3x2−6xy)i−(6xy−3y2)j)⋅(i−j)=03x2−6xy+6xy−3y2=03x2−3y2=0x2−y2=0(x−y)(x+y)=0

Therefore, x=y or x=−y. Substituting x=y into the equation of our curve gives:

3yx2=48+3xy23yy2=48+3yy23y3=48+3y30=48

Since we get a false statement, we conclude that does not exist points of the form (x,x) on the curve. Substituting x=−y into the equation of our curve gives:

3yx2=48+3xy23y(−y)2=48+3(−y)y23y3=48−3y36y3=48y3=8y=83y=2

Finally:

  • If y=2, we get x=−2 and the corresponding point is (−2,2).
